passages.t: Zophar: the triumph of the wicked is brief
passages.happening:
‘Then Zophar the Naamathite replied’ (verse 1). “So my anxious thoughts compel me to answer, because of the turmoil within me. I have heard a rebuke that insults me” (verses 2-3).

“Do you not know that from antiquity, since man was placed on the earth, the triumph of the wicked has been brief and the joy of the godless momentary?” (verses 4-5). His pride may reach the heavens, but he will perish like his own dung, and those who saw him will ask where he is. He flies away like a dream. His sons will have to beg favor from the poor, and his own hands will give back his wealth. His youthful strength will lie down with him in the dust.
passages.hearers:
In chapter 19 Job reached the astonishing confidence that his Redeemer lives, and he warned the friends that their persecution would bring judgment on them. Zophar hears only the warning, and he answers it. He does not answer Job's hope at all.

This is Zophar's last speech in the book. In the third round he is never given a turn, and the friends' voice runs out.

His case, in the form he would sign: it has always been so, everywhere, since the first man. The world has a moral order, and the wicked come down, and quickly. Across the ancient Near East, wisdom writers taught the same, and so do many of Israel's own proverbs and psalms. Zophar is not inventing a doctrine. He is defending the consensus of his world, and he assumes that anyone who questions it has abandoned wisdom itself.

Godless, chaneph, in verse 5 describes someone whose piety is hollow. By implication Zophar places Job in that company.
passages.later: A psalm says much the same, as a lesson learned over a lifetime: “I have seen a wicked, ruthless man flourishing like a well-rooted native tree, yet he passed away and was no more” (Psalm 37:35-36).
passages.asks: Zophar heard Job's warning and missed his hope. Ask whether you listen for the part of someone's words that wounds you, and miss the rest. And ask what you would have said to a man who had just said his Redeemer lives.

passages.t: Sweet in the mouth, poison in the stomach
passages.happening:
Evil is sweet in the wicked man's mouth, and he keeps it under his tongue. ‘Yet in his stomach his food sours into the venom of cobras within him. He swallows wealth but vomits it out; God will force it from his stomach’ (verses 14-15). He will not enjoy the rivers of honey and cream.

Why? ‘For he has oppressed and forsaken the poor; he has seized houses he did not build’ (verse 19). His appetite is never satisfied. ‘When he has filled his stomach, God will vent His fury upon him, raining it down on him as he eats’ (verse 23). He flees an iron weapon and a bronze arrow strikes him. Fire consumes what is left in his tent. ‘The heavens will expose his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him’ (verse 27).

“This is the wicked man’s portion from God, the inheritance God has appointed him” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Zophar's pictures keep returning to eating: sweetness in the mouth, food that sours, wealth swallowed and vomited, an appetite never filled, and finally God's anger raining down on the man as he eats. Ancient people commonly thought snake venom came from the gall, and the Hebrew word for gall in verse 14 is linked with bitterness and poison. Rivers of honey and cream were a byword for plenty, close to Israel's own words for the promised land.

Verse 19 names the crime: oppressing the poor and seizing their houses. A powerful man could foreclose on debtors and take their homes, and the prophets and wisdom writers condemn it again and again. Zophar is right that this is wicked.

Notice what is missing. After the opening, Zophar never speaks to Job directly, and he never mentions turning back to God. The door he left open in chapter 11 has closed.

Portion and inheritance in verse 29 are good words, words for a share of land handed down. Zophar turns them bitter: the only share the wicked man leaves is ruin.
passages.later: The Psalms use Zophar's word portion for the faithful, with the opposite meaning: “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; You have made my lot secure” (Psalm 16:5).
passages.hard:
Much of what Zophar says sounds like the Bible's own teaching. Why is he wrong?

The difficulty is real. Psalms such as 37 and 73, and many proverbs, also say that the wicked are brief and that God brings them down, and the prophets condemn the same oppression of the poor that Zophar names. Readers have answered in several ways. One answer is that Zophar's error lies in his certainty about timing: he claims the fall is always swift and visible, which Job and much of Scripture deny. Psalm 73 itself begins with the prosperity of the wicked. Another is that the error is one of application: a general truth about how God governs the world is turned into a diagnosis of a particular sufferer, and in Job's case the diagnosis is false. A third observes that Zophar speaks without compassion and without listening, so that even true words become a weapon.

These answers work together. The book's verdict comes in 42:7, where God says the friends have not spoken rightly about him, as Job has. True sentences can still misrepresent God when they are used to accuse someone in pain.
passages.asks: Zophar described greed truly and applied it falsely. Ask whether there is greed in your own life that his words should reach. And ask whether you have ever turned a true warning into an accusation against someone who did not deserve it.
